Learning Objectives
Recognize the role of implant design and its effects on kinematics in total knee arthroplasty.
Describe strategies to manage the posterior cruciate ligament in total knee arthroplasty,
including retention, substitution, or sacrifice.
Discuss how management of the posterior cruciate ligament is associated with specific implant
and bearing designs.
Assess design rationales for emerging bearing options, including anterior-stabilized and pivot
bearings.
Recognize and determine indications for and outcomes of the use of varus-valgus constrained
implants in total knee arthroplasty.
Review modern cementless fixation as an option for total knee arthroplasty in select patients.

Overview
Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) designs continue to evolve:
Design rationales seek to improve patient satisfaction and function postoperatively.
Various levels of constraint and strategies exist for the management of the posterior cruciate
ligament (PCL), which is reflected in various design options.
Knowledge of how these designs may affect knee kinematics and outcomes after TKA is
important.

Overview
In the United States, TKA is a common and successful procedure for the management
of knee arthritis. Ninety percent of patients experience a considerable reduction in
pain after TKA, and, for most patients, this leads to higher quality of life and improved
mobility.1 However, approximately 20% of patients report dissatisfaction after TKA.2
This has led to continued efforts to make advances in implant designs, providing
surgeons with various options to use in TKA. (Resource 1)
Femoral Component Design
Modern femoral component designs are based on the Total Condylar Knee, the forerunner of
modern TKA designs.
Broadly, femoral component designs differ in two main design characteristics
Posterior-stabilized designs versus cruciate-retaining designs
Single-radius, multi-radius, or gradually reducing radius designs (Figure 1)


Femoral Component Design
The tibiofemoral articulation maintains stability through a relationship of static and
dynamic forces. The anatomy of the articular surfaces, specifically the circumference and
radii of the femoral condyles in the sagittal plane, contributes to the static stability of the
articulation and plays a key role in native knee kinematics (Resource 2). Many TKA design
rationales aim to simulate normal knee kinematics; however, TKA designs have
kinematic limitations associated with functional limitations and, potentially, patient
dissatisfaction. Noble et al3 reported that patients who undergo TKA have difficulty
performing activities such as kneeling, carrying loads, playing tennis, dancing, and
gardening compared with age-matched peers. In addition, in vivo studies demonstrate
abnormal knee kinematic profiles after TKA.4-7 New implant designs; improved surgical
techniques; improved instrumentation; and, potentially, navigation or robotics may
result in more normal knee kinematics and decreased patient dissatisfaction rates.
Understanding the history of TKA design is important; surgeons must be aware of the
considerations and new developments related to implant geometry and bearing designs
(Video 1).

In 1974, the Total Condylar Knee was introduced; the prosthesis featured a femoral
component with a trochlear groove and included multiple radii of curvature.8 By 1976,
the design had advanced to the Total Condylar III, the predecessor of all future posterior-
stabilized TKA designs.9 Posterior stabilization was achieved via placement of a femoral
cam and tibial post (Figure 2). Broadly, femoral cam designs are classified as an open-
box design with a bridge-style connection between the posterior condyles or a closed-
box design between the condyles of the femur. In early posterior-stabilized designs, the
post and cam were placed symmetrically, with the post centrally in the polyethylene and
the cam spanning the posterior femoral condyles10 (Resources 3 and 4)
Figure 2 Illustration shows cam and post interaction. A cam that is positioned at the top
and most posterior aspect of the femoral posterior condyles will tend to interact with the
tibial post later in the flexion arc, but it will tend to remain at the base of the post in the
extremes of flexion, thereby maximizing the jump height of the cam on the post. As the
cam moves anteriorly across the box (dark circle), the interaction will tend to occur
earlier in flexion and will articulate higher on the post late in the flexion arc, thereby
decreasing the jump height. (Reproduced from Mihalko WM: Kinematics in total knee
arthroplasty, in Mont MA, Tanzer M, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Hip and Knee, ed

The Continuum of Constraint in TKA
Cruciate-retaining bearings
Mild to moderate deformity with an intact and functional PCL
Pivot bearings: medial-pivot, medial-constrained, medial-congruent, or dual-pivot
Mild to moderate deformity with balanced collateral ligaments, plus or minus PCL retention
or sacrifice
Anterior-stabilized bearings: ultracongruent, deep-dished, or condylar-stabilized
Mild to moderate deformity with an attenuated or nonfunctional PCL
Posterior-stabilized bearings

Varus-valgus constrained

Hinged TKA


The Continuum of Constraint in TKA
Debate continues among surgeons and in the literature regarding management of the
PCL in TKA.11-13 Advocates of posterior-stabilized designs argue that these designs offer
a more reproducible kinematic profile with potentially increased range of motion and
that they can be used to correct larger deformities if balancing a PCL may not be
possible (Figure 3). In a 1990 classic study, Laskin9 reviewed the results of 80 patients
who underwent TKA with the use of a Total Condylar Knee prosthesis. Despite limited
size options, primitive instrumentation, and patients with rheumatoid arthritis and
considerable deformities, Laskin reported promising outcomes, especially compared
with previous designs. The success of the Total Condylar Knee followed by the Insall-
Burstein I and II prostheses, all with posterior-stabilized designs, has led to continued
use of posterior-stabilized designs in the United States.10 The 2020 annual report of the
American Joint Replacement Registry showed relatively consistent use of posterior-
stabilized TKA designs in the United States from 2012 to 2019, with a peak use of 52.5%
in 201614 (Figure 4). Conversely, the Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint
Replacement Registry reported a decline in the use of posterior-stabilized TKA designs
from 32.9% in 2008 to 20.5% in 2018,15 and the 2020 annual report of the National Joint
Registry of the United Kingdom showed a 20% use of posterior-stabilized TKA designs in
2019.16

stabilized total knee arthroplasty implant. The tibial post engages a femoral box during

gaps are not balanced) may cause failure of the total knee arthroplasty implant.

Functionally, the PCL provides a restraining force against posterior translation of the
tibia relative to the femur, and it supports stability of the knee in flexion.17 In cruciate-
retaining TKA, conservation of the PCL reduces posterior translation of the tibia and
contributes to femoral rollback in knee flexion.18,19 (Resource 5)
Advocates of cruciate-retaining TKA cite potential advantages of fewer patellar
complications, a reduction in shear forces at the bone-tibial implant interface, more
bone-conserving femoral designs (no need to resect intercondylar bone from the femur
to accommodate the box and cam), and improved proprioception with retained
mechanoreceptors in the native PCL.20 In addition, eliminating the femoral box resection

9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Implant Designs in Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001030
8/27

may decrease intraoperative fracture risk because distal femur fractures have been
reported as a result of improper intercondylar notch osteotomies or box sizes.21
Kinematic fluoroscopic studies that compare cruciate-retaining and posterior-stabilized
TKA designs have been performed.5-7,22 Neither posterior-stabilized nor cruciate-
retaining TKA designs exactly replicate normal kinematics; however, some key variations
between these designs were noted. Cruciate-retaining designs may show paradoxical
anterior or forward sliding of the femoral component on the tibial bearing; this is most
noted during lunge or squatting-type maneuvers.23 Posterior-stabilized designs tend to
show more consistent kinematics; however, the kinematics are not comparable to
normal knee motion. Posterior-stabilized designs tend to have more anterior position of
the femoral component at full extension. In the transverse plane, posterior-stabilized
and cruciate-retaining designs have shown that 25% or more of patients experience
internal tibial rotation with respect to the femur during flexion; this has been suggested
to be a risk factor for patient dissatisfaction.6 Despite arguments in favor of cruciate-
retaining or posterior-stabilized TKA, several studies report no difference in functional
outcome between these two designs.12,24,25
Alternative Tibial Bearing Designs
Ultracongruent, or Anterior-Stabilized, Bearings

Ultracongruent, or Anterior-Stabilized, Bearings
A more recent, highly conforming TKA bearing with an elevated anterior lip and a
deepened dish has emerged as an innovation for PCL substitution. These bearings have
been termed anterior stabilized, condylar-stabilized, deep-dish congruent, or
ultracongruent, with subtle differences based on the manufacturer. Some implant-
specific differences exist based on manufacturer specifications, including the amount of
elevation of the anterior and posterior lips and the level of congruency; however, these
highly congruent bearings are broadly termed anterior-stabilized bearings (Video 2).
The highly conforming anterior buildup increases the contact with the femoral
component throughout full range of motion (Figure 5). The anterior buildup increases

Anterior-stabilized bearings offer several potential advantages. They allow for ease and
speed of conversion to substitute for a PCL deemed incompetent or poorly balanced
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Implant Designs in Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001030
11/27

during placement of a cruciate-retaining femoral component design. In addition,
because of the use of a cruciate-retaining femoral component design, anterior-stabilized
bearings are bone preserving, which allows the trochlear notch in the femoral
component to extend distally, potentially preventing patellar clunk. Finally, using only
one type of femoral component decreases inventory requirements.
Previous evaluations describing the kinematics of anterior-stabilized bearings alone or
compared with posterior-stabilized bearings have shown similar results. An evaluation of
anterior-posterior displacement of tibiofemoral contact points found that use of an
anterior-stabilized bearing reduced posterior displacements without a consequence on
range of motion; however, some paradoxical displacements were detected.27 An
intraoperative kinematic evaluation found that anterior-stabilized designs have more
pronounced paradoxical anterior translation, decreased posterior rollback, and
decreased range of motion compared with posterior-stabilized designs.28 A similar
investigation comparing anterior- and posterior-stabilized bearing designs also found
similar intraoperative anterior-posterior displacement; however, the investigators noted
that neither reproduced physiologic kinematics, and they found no difference in
postoperative range of motion or patient-reported outcomes (PROs).29
Despite the increased anterior-posterior displacement noted in the kinematic studies
comparing anterior-stabilized to posterior-stabilized bearing designs, clinical outcomes
essentially have been equivalent. Multiple prospective randomized clinical trials have
compared the results of anterior- and posterior-stabilized bearing designs. Scott30
reported equivalent outcomes at a final follow-up of 5 years, with the anterior-stabilized
group reporting considerably fewer incidences of postoperative mechanical sensations
potentially related to patellar clunk. Four other prospective randomized controlled trials
have compared clinical outcomes, patient satisfaction, and radiographic outcomes
between anterior- and posterior-stabilized bearing designs without any noted
differences.31-34
Three separate retrospective clinical series have compared anterior-stabilized and
cruciate-retaining bearing designs with varying results. Emerson et al35 compared 424
knees in which TKA was performed with the use of an anterior-stabilized bearing with
930 knees in which TKA was performed with the use of cruciate-retaining bearings,

Peters et al36 compared 228 knees in which TKA was performed with the use of anterior-
stabilized bearings with 240 knees in which TKA was performed with the use of cruciate-
retaining bearings, reporting no difference in PROs, radiographic outcomes, component
loosening, manipulation rate, or major complications; however, the authors noted that
the cruciate-retaining group had considerably more revision procedures. Similarly,
Hofmann et al30 compared anterior-stabilized and cruciate-retaining TKA and reported
similar range of motion and PROs; however, the authors noted more revision
procedures in the cruciate-retaining group compared with the anterior-stabilized group.
Medial-Pivot, Medial-Stabilized, and Medial-Congruent Bearings

Medial-Pivot, Medial-Stabilized, and Medial-Congruent Bearings
An alternative emerging TKA bearing design, termed the medial-pivot, medial-stabilized,
or medial-congruent bearing, involves the use of a conforming medial compartment
articulation similar to a ball-and-socket design with a flat lateral compartment design
(Figure 6). This design allows the lateral condyle to move more freely throughout the arc
of flexion and extension of the knee to re-create more normal native knee kinematics.
This design has been available and in use since 1994; however, its popularity recently
has increased, with more manufacturers producing this type of design37 (Video 3).
Figure 6 Image shows a medial-pivot bearing, which uses a conforming medial
compartment articulation similar to a ball-and-socket design with a flat lateral

The medial-pivot bearing design shares many of the potential advantages of anterior-
stabilized bearings because of the use of a cruciate-retaining femoral component. In
addition, the design offers the potential to create more natural knee kinematics and for
the surgeon to choose to retain or sacrifice the PCL with the same medial-pivot
bearing.38 Despite the desire to re-create medial-pivot kinematics of normal knees,
whether re-creating a medial-pivot pattern based on intraoperative kinematics is
associated with improved patient outcomes remains on. Warth et al39 evaluated a
cohort of 141 TKA procedures and noted a medial-pivot kinematic pattern in 40% of the
TKA procedures with no improvement in outcomes. Conversely, Nishio et al40 evaluated
40 TKA procedures via a CT-based navigation system and noted that a medial-pivot
kinematic pattern resulted in improved functional activities, patient satisfaction, and
knee flexion angles.

Compared with posterior-stabilized bearing designs, the medial-pivot bearing design is
associated with similar results and some potential advantages. In a randomized
controlled trial comparing posterior-stabilized and medial-pivot bearings, Hossain et al37
reported similar relief in pain and improved function; however, the medial-pivot group
had better high-end function. Similarly, Kulshrestha et al41 evaluated early outcomes of
medial-pivot versus posterior-stabilized designs and noted similar PROs between the
two groups but improved timed-up-and-go and self-paced walk tests in the medial-pivot
group. In addition, Samy et al42 retrospectively compared medial-pivot and posterior-
stabilized designs and found that patients with a medial-pivot TKA design had improved
forgotten joint scores. Outcomes information comparing cruciate-retaining designs and
medial-pivot designs is limited; one registry study from Norway and Australia suggested
the potential for decreased survival of the medial-pivot design compared with cruciate-
retaining designs.43
Dual-Pivot Bearings

Dual-Pivot Bearings
Another newer bearing option is the dual-pivot design, which attempts to replicate an
early-flexion lateral-pivot and late-flexion medial-pivot kinematic pattern. This kinematic
pattern most resembles native knees with an intact anterior cruciate ligament. The dual-
pivot bearing attempts to achieve this kinematic pattern with the use of a conforming
lateral compartment, attempting to drive an early lateral-pivot motion in early flexion;
the medial compartment polyethylene also is conforming to a degree but less than the
lateral side.44 Re-creating this dual-pivot kinematic pattern via intraoperative sensor
measurements has been associated with improved PROs and patient satisfaction
scores;45 however, reports of outcomes with the use of this design are limited.
Additional studies comparing the results to of cruciate-retaining, anterior-stabilized, and
posterior-stabilized bearings are necessary.


Varus-Valgus Constrained TKA
In general, the least amount of constraint is selected for TKA because increasing the level
of constraint may sacrifice more bone, increase stress on the implants, and decrease
range of motion.46 In certain situations during complex primary TKA and during revision
TKA, additional constraint may be necessary. In these situations, a varus-valgus
constrained bearing design may be an option to provide additional stability. Because
instability remains a common cause of aseptic failure after TKA, knowledge of the design
indications and outcomes for the use of bearings with additional constraint is important.
Instability has been reported to be the second most common indication for revision TKA
(18.7%), following aseptic loosening (31.2%). 47 (Figure 7).

Varus-valgus constrained bearings are modifications of posterior-stabilized bearings with
a larger and more conforming tibial post that engages a deeper and occasionally wider
femoral box to provide additional constraint in the coronal plate.48 Relative indications
for the use of varus-valgus constrained designs have been suggested: valgus deformity
with laxity of the MCL.49 severe flexion contracture with inability to balance ligaments,50
varus-valgus laxity greater than 5 mm throughout range of motion,51 advanced extra-
articular deformity,52 and neuropathic arthropathy.53
Intermediate-term follow-up studies have found satisfactory results with the use of
varus-valgus constrained designs, with survivorship as high as 97.6% at a minimum
follow-up of 7 years.51 Similarly, another cohort study of varus-valgus constrained TKA
reported no aseptic failures at a mean follow-up of 12.7 years.54 These studies and other
studies are limited in size and follow-up duration and often evaluate only one implant
design. The use of varus-valgus designs during complex primary TKA has been suggested
to increase all-cause revisions at long-term follow-up.51 With increasing stress at the
implant-bone interface or at the bone-cement interface because of the use of varus-
valgus implants, surgeons should consider using additional intramedullary stems. This
remains controversial, with some studies advocate for the use of additional
intramedullary stems55 and other studies reporting similar outcomes without the use of
additional intramedullary stems.56
Cementless TKA

Cementless TKA
Modern highly porous surfaces have helped increase confidence and the use of
cementless TKA in the United States. Potential advantages of cementless TKA include
bone preservation during revision surgery, elimination of third-body wear from cement
debris, and shorter surgical time.57

9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Implant Designs in Total Knee Arthroplasty
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001030
18/27

Early generations of cementless TKA designs were associated with increased risks of
failure and poor clinical outcomes.58,59 These early generation cementless TKA failures
generally were attributed to failure of the cementless patellar or tibial components.60-62
Retrieval analyses of early generation tibial components revealed levels of
osseointegration lower than 30%.63 Improvement in the design of the patellofemoral
articulation and the elimination of thin polyethylene and sharp metal borders have led
to improved results.64 The decreasing popularity of patellar resurfacing and the
introduction of modern highly porous surfaces have tempered concerns for patellar- or
tibial-related failure. These design improvements have led to a relatively rapid increase
in cementless TKA in the United States, increasing from 1.9% in 2012 to 20.5% in 2022
according to the American Joint Replacement Registry.65
Modern generation cementless tibial and patellar components include those with highly
porous metals.66,67 This includes those with porous tantalum68 or highly porous
titanium69 and those that involve the use of three-dimensional printing or electron-
beam melting.70,71 This is in contrast to older generation tibial and patellar components,
which included cobalt-chromium sintered beads, titanium fiber metal mesh, cancellous-
structured titanium, or titanium plasma spray surfaces.
Recent prospective and retrospective studies on modern cementless TKA have reported
no differences in survivorship and lower rates of aseptic loosening in select patient
populations compared with cemented TKA;57,72-75 however, these studies are limited in
their power to detect revision risk and specific mechanisms of failure, including
mechanical loosening, and in their generalizability to the United States experience. In the
United States, the American Joint Replacement Registry has reported no difference in the
associated risk of revision with select use of cementless fixation for TKA.76 This differs
from international registry studies, which suggest an increased risk of failure with
cementless fixation. The Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement
Registry is most similar to the United States with regard to the use of cementless fixation
for TKA, with approximately 20% of TKA procedures performed in 2022 being
cementless.77 The Australian Orthopaedic Association National Joint Replacement
Registry 2023 Annual Report reported an increased cumulative percent revision with
cementless TKA compared with cemented TKA if a cruciate-retaining femoral component
